Transmitted from Arabic sources into Latin Europe through 12th-century translations (Hugo of Santalla, Gerard of Cremona), geomancy became the most systematic of the non-astrological divination arts — precise, teachable, and defensible as natural philosophy. Its companion arts, chiromancy (palmistry) and physiognomy (face-reading), share its diagnostic, text-plus-diagram format. Together these arts produced one of the richest manuscript illustration traditions in medieval and Renaissance Europe: elaborate figure charts, body maps, and casting diagrams survive in hundreds of manuscripts from Paris to Prague. The geomantic tradition also extends far beyond Europe: Arabic *'ilm al-raml* remains a living practice, West African Ifa divination shares the same 16-figure binary logic (as the 256 *odu* of Ifa), and Malagasy *sikidy* preserves the oldest continuous geomantic practice outside the Arab world.

title: The Necromantic Manuscript Tradition & Trithemius
creator: various; Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516)
rights: Public domain / CC BY / CC BY-SA (per item). Via Wikimedia Commons.
blurb: The 15th-century clerical underworld of 'illicit learned magic' (Richard Kieckhefer's term) produced manuscripts like the Munich Handbook of Necromancy (Clm 849) — practical guides combining liturgical Latin, astrological timing, and outright demon-summoning, written by literate clergy for clergy. Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Benedictine abbot of Sponheim and teacher of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, sits at the hinge between this clerical-necromantic tradition and Renaissance ceremonial magic: his cryptographic *Steganographia* (claimed to be angel-magic, later shown to be cipher theory) and his angelic hierarchies of planetary intelligences extend the older astral-image tradition of Thabit ibn Qurra's *De Imaginibus* into the print era.

title: Calcination & Congelation: Process Imagery
creator: various
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
blurb: Supplementary imagery for the two most visually underrepresented of the twelve alchemical operations: calcination (reduction to ash by fire — the first work, governed by Saturn) and congelation (fixation of the volatile into solid form — the binding of spirit into body).

title: Islamic Talismanic Objects: Shirts, Scrolls, Bowls and Amulets
creator: various
place: Ottoman Empire; Iran; Egypt; Islamic world
rights: Public Domain; CC0; CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO. Via Wikimedia Commons.
blurb: Physical talismans from the Islamic world: Ottoman and Safavid-era shirts inscribed top-to-bottom with Quranic verses, divine names, magic squares (wafq), and zodiacal symbols; prayer scrolls; brass talismanic bowls with serpent-and-zodiac ornament. These wearable and portable objects embody the practical side of the learned Islamic occult tradition documented in texts like the Picatrix, al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif, and the Solomonic seal literature.

title: Barchusen — Elementa Chemiae (Utrecht, 1718): Alchemical Emblem Plates
creator: Johann Conrad Barchusen
rights: CC0. Via Wikimedia Commons / Science History Institute, Philadelphia.
blurb: The 78 copper-engraved emblem plates from Johann Conrad Barchusen's encyclopedic Elementa Chemiae (Utrecht, 1718), derived directly from a manuscript of The Crowning of Nature (Coronatio Naturae). These engravings represent the first and only major printed edition of the Crowning of Nature emblem sequence, depicting the stages of the philosopher's stone through sequential allegorical images: toad, dragon, crowned king and queen, alchemical vessel, putrefaction, conjunction, multiplication, and projection.

title: Thomas Norton — Ordinal of Alchemy (c. 1477): Manuscripts and 1652 Printed Plates
creator: Thomas Norton
rights: Public Domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
blurb: The Ordinal of Alchemy (Ordinal of Alchimy) composed by the Bristol alchemist Thomas Norton c. 1477, the most important verse treatise on alchemy in Middle English. Written in rhyming couplets, the Ordinal describes the philosophical and practical stages of the Great Work through seven chapters, from the election of the alchemist to the perfection of the Stone. The work survives in seventeen manuscripts and was first printed with engraved plates in Elias Ashmole's Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (1652).

title: Hildegard of Bingen — Scivias and Liber Divinorum Operum Illuminations
creator: Hildegard of Bingen
rights: Public Domain (pre-1928). Eibingen facsimile via Yorck Project (GFDL).
blurb: The illuminated visionary manuscripts of Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), Benedictine abbess, theologian, composer, and doctor of the Church. Her two major illustrated works — Scivias (Know the Ways, c. 1151) and Liber Divinorum Operum (Book of Divine Works, c. 1163–73) — contain some of the most extraordinary cosmological imagery of the medieval period: an egg-shaped universe of concentric spheres, mandala-like diagrams of the Trinity, a cosmic man standing in the center of creation, and elaborate angel-hierarchies. The Scivias illuminations survive primarily through a 1927 hand-made facsimile (Eibingen Abbey) of the lost Rupertsberg Codex.

title: Shams al-Ma'arif — The Sun of Knowledge (Ahmad al-Buni)
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni
place: North Africa / Egypt (composed); later MS origin unknown
rights: Public Domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL).
blurb: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni's (d. 622/1225) Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra (The Great Sun of Knowledge) is the most influential Arabic grimoire and the foundational text of Islamicate lettrism (huruf). It systematizes the occult properties of the 28 Arabic letters, the 99 Names of God, magic squares (awfaq), and planetary talismans into a vast cosmological system. Buni synthesizes Sufi cosmology, astrological magic, and Neoplatonic letter-mysticism into a practical manual for divine invocation and natural magic. The text circulated in hundreds of manuscript copies across the Islamic world from Morocco to Central Asia, and was central to the practices of Sufi orders, court magicians, and popular healers alike.

title: Shams al-Ma'arif — Manuscript Copy (c. 1500 CE)
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. 622/1225 CE)
date: c. 1500 CE (MS copy); text composed c. 1200–1225 CE
place: North Africa or Egypt (probable MS origin)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE, over 100 years old. Scan via Internet Archive.
blurb: A manuscript copy of Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra (The Great Sun of Knowledge), dating to approximately 1500 CE. Unlike the printed Cairo edition, this manuscript is written in red and black ink with extensive red-ink decoration: chapter headings in large thuluth script inside ruled frames, inline magic squares (awfaq) with Arabic letters and numbers drawn in red, cosmological circle diagrams, star-khatim talisman seals, and full-page letter grids. The manuscript demonstrates the living tradition of Buniyan lettrism — the systematic application of the Arabic alphabet's occult properties to generate protective and invocatory seals, talismanic diagrams, and cosmological schemata. The red-ink style is characteristic of North African and Egyptian manuscripts in the Mamluk-Ottoman period (15th–16th c.), when the Shams al-Ma'arif circulated most widely. Digitized as part of the Internet Archive's Islamic Manuscripts collection.

title: Islamic Geomancy (Raml) — Instruments, Manuscripts, and Diagrams
creator: various
rights: Public Domain / CC (per item). Via Wikimedia Commons and Wellcome Collection.
blurb: Geomancy (Arabic: 'ilm al-raml, the science of sand) is an Islamicate divination system in which binary marks in sand generate 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), which are then combined into a shield chart (al-darb) to answer questions about the future. Originally derived from African divination practices and transmitted into the Islamic world, raml was systematized by scholars including al-Kindi, Tumtum al-Hindi, and later encyclopedists. Al-Buni integrates raml into his talismanic system: the 16 geomantic figures correspond to Arabic letters, planets, and divine Names, connecting sand divination to the broader Islamic occult sciences. This work collects key visual sources: the earliest dated geomantic instrument (British Museum, 1241/42 CE), manuscript pages from the Wellcome Library's Arabic treatise on geomancy (MS Arabic 823), and diagrammatic classifications of the 16 figures.

title: Shams al-Ma'arif wa-Lata'if al-'Awarif — Princeton MS Garrett 258Y (1468 CE)
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. 622/1225 CE)
rights: Public Domain. Digitized by Princeton University Library under IIIF open access.
blurb: A short recension of al-Buni's encyclopaedia of occult sciences, copied in 1468 CE (872 AH). Princeton University Library, Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 258Y (133 leaves). Acquired from the collection of Abraham Shalom Yahuda; gift of Robert Garrett, Class of 1897, 1942. The manuscript contains the abbreviated form of the Shams al-Ma'arif with embedded awfaq (magic-square) tables and letter grids. This compact recension illustrates how al-Buni's system was transmitted in condensed practical form: the diagrammatic content is embedded directly in the text flow rather than displayed as full-page illustrations.

title: Bulugh al-Watar fi Usul Ilm al-Athar — Geomancy Treatise (Princeton, Garrett)
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public Domain — manuscript (date unknown). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A manuscript treatise on geomancy (ilm al-raml) held at Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection), 20 leaves (40 pages). The title Bulugh al-Watar fi Usul Ilm al-Athar (Attaining the Desire in the Principles of the Science of Traces/Marks) refers to geomancy, which in Arabic is literally the 'science of the trace' — marks left in sand or earth by the diviner's stylus. The treatise comprises an introduction, five chapters (abwab) and a conclusion, discussing the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), their names, properties, and the system of the geomantic house-chart (bayt). The text integrates the geomantic figures with humoral and planetary properties, and contains inline geomantic figure notations (the distinctive 1-or-2-dot-per-row patterns) embedded within the text columns. This compact treatise represents the concise, practical wing of the Arabic geomancy literature — focused on the operational system rather than philosophical elaboration.

title: Grimoire, 18th Century — Italian Occult Compendium (Princeton)
creator: Anonymous (Italian, 18th century)
rights: Public Domain — 18th century manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: An 18th-century Italian occult compendium (20 leaves, paper, 15 × 21.4 cm) held at Princeton University Library. It combines ritual recipes, ceremonial magic, alchemy, astrology, and demonology in a single manuscript. The volume is remarkable for its illustrations: magical alphabets (including the Transitus Fluvii / Crossing the River script, a standard late-medieval magical alphabet derived from Hebrew), Hebrew kamea (magic squares) with angelic names, circular spirit seals in the tradition of Solomonic magic, SATOR-style letter word-squares, and a faint planetary/astrological grid. The Latin and Italian text draws on multiple grimoire traditions — Solomonic, Agrippan, and folk magical — blending them into a practical working manual. The Hebrew magical alphabets and seals indicate the author's access to the learned Kabbalah-infused ceremonial magic tradition transmitted through works like Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (1531) and the Key of Solomon manuscripts.

title: Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf — Huruf MS (Princeton, 15th c.)
creator: Kumi, Muhammad ibn Muhammad (active 15th century)
rights: Public Domain — 15th century manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A 15th-century Arabic manuscript on 'ilm al-huruf (the science of letters), 112 leaves (232 pages), held at Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection). The work is Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf (Facilitating Goals in the Secrets of Letters) by Kumi Muhammad ibn Muhammad (active 15th century), followed by a second text on the degrees of power of the letters. The manuscript contains extensive tables and charts: magic squares (awfaq) with red-bordered grids, including a spectacular full-page 8×8 wafq thaman (Jupiter magic square), as well as smaller letter-number grids and combinatorial tables of letter values (huruf al-abjad). 'Ilm al-huruf — Islamic lettrism or letter science — holds that the 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet are the structural elements of creation, each carrying elemental, planetary, numerical (abjad), and divine-name correspondences. Practitioners use letter combinations, awfaq, and name-analysis to generate talismans, predict outcomes, and decode the hidden structure of words. The Princeton MS represents the rich 15th-century tradition of learned Islamic letter science in the tradition of al-Buni, Ibn Khaldun, and the Ikhwan al-Safa.

title: Majmuah Rasail Nadira fi Ulum al-Falakiyah — Astronomical Treatise Collection (Princeton, Garrett)
creator: Multiple authors (anthology)
rights: Public Domain — medieval manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: An 870-page collection of rare astronomical and mathematical treatises in Arabic, Persian, and Ottoman Turkish, held at Princeton University Library (Robert Garrett Collection). The full title is Majmuat al-Rasail al-Nadira fi Ulum al-Falakiyah (Collection of Rare Treatises on the Sciences of the Spheres/Astronomy). The 433-leaf manuscript contains numerous distinct texts beginning with: geometry, astronomy (ilm al-hay'a), astronomical tables (zij), star catalogs, mathematical calculations, and related sciences. The manuscript is decorated with gold-bordered astronomical tables (jadawil) — systematic charts for star positions, solar and lunar corrections, planetary equations, and calendar calculations. These tables represent the operational core of Islamic mathematical astronomy: the practitioner (astronomer, astrologer, muwaqqit) consulted them to compute planetary positions for a given date and to interpret astrological charts. The Garrett collection copy was donated by Robert Garrett (1875–1961) and constitutes one of Princeton's most important Arabic scientific manuscripts.

title: Sharh Samarat Batlamyus — Ptolemy Commentary by Tusi (Princeton, Garrett Collection)
creator: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript (pre-modern). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A Princeton University Library manuscript (Garrett Collection) containing two Persian astronomical-astrological texts by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274), totaling 128 leaves (136 pages as digitized). The first text (fols. 3a–53a) is Sharh Samarat Batlamyus (Commentary on the Fruits/Centiloquium of Ptolemy) — a Persian translation of and commentary on the pseudo-Ptolemaic Centiloquium (100 astrological aphorisms) attributed to Ptolemy, with al-Tusi's explanatory notes. The second text is a further astrological work by al-Tusi. The manuscript contains astronomical and astrological diagrams including a circular epicycle or armillary-sphere diagram with Arabic/Persian labels indicating planetary positions and celestial mechanics. Al-Tusi (the Ilkhanid court astronomer at Maragha) was the most important Islamic astronomer of the 13th century, producing revised planetary tables (Zij-i Ilkhani) and corrections to Ptolemy's Almagest that were foundational for both Islamic astronomy and the later Copernican revolution.

title: Ripley Alchemical Scroll — Princeton (Smethley Copy, c. 1570)
creator: George Ripley (attr.); Leonard Smethley (scribe/artist)
rights: Public Domain — 16th century manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: An illustrated alchemical roll incorporating Middle English verses attributed to Sir George Ripley (d. c.1490), copied by Leonard Smethley. The scroll is composed of seven parchment membranes totaling 3720 × 275 mm, painted with alchemical roundels, figures, and symbolic sequences depicting the stages of the Great Work: putrefaction, dissolution, conjunction, multiplication, and projection. Figures include the crowned king and queen, the Green Lion, the pelican feeding its young with its blood, the Red Man and White Woman (Sulphur and Mercury), serpents, and alchemical vessels. The Ripley Scroll is one of the most visually distinctive documents in early modern English alchemy, surviving in multiple manuscript copies (Princeton, Huntington, Getty, Yale). It synthesizes Ripley's Compound of Alchymie (1471) into a continuous visual narrative: reading from top to bottom, it stages the alchemical process as a royal drama of death, marriage, and resurrection. This copy is attributed to Leonard Smethley and held at Princeton University Library.

title: Ripley Alchemical Scroll — Princeton Taylor Collection (c. 1580)
creator: George Ripley (attr.)
rights: Public Domain — 16th century manuscript. Princeton University Library (Taylor Collection).
blurb: A second Ripley alchemical roll held at Princeton University Library, from the Robert H. Taylor Collection. Like the companion scroll (princeton_ripley1), it is a painted parchment roll incorporating Middle English verses attributed to Sir George Ripley (d. c.1490) and alchemical roundels depicting the stages of the Great Work. This copy was acquired through dealers H.P. Kraus and Laurence Witten and gifted to Princeton by Robert H. Taylor (1908–1985). Multiple copies of the Ripley Scroll survive in English and American collections (Princeton, Huntington, Getty, Yale), testifying to the scroll's popularity as both a practical alchemical guide and a prestigious object in 16th–17th-century English culture. Each copy introduces subtle pictorial variations, making comparison between copies a research tool for tracking the transmission of alchemical iconography.

title: Al-Shajara al-Muthimara — Geomancy Treatise (Princeton, Garrett Collection)
creator: Khalaf al-Barbari
rights: Public Domain — manuscript (date unknown). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A manuscript treatise on geomancy (ilm al-raml — the science of sand) by Khalaf al-Barbari, 46 leaves (92 pages), illustrated with tables and diagrams, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection). The full title is al-Shajara al-Muthimara li-Taysir al-Nuqta al-Mu'tabara (The Fruitful Tree for Facilitating the Respected Point). Geomancy (ilm al-raml) is a divination system based on 16 binary figures (each composed of 4 rows of 1 or 2 points) that was transmitted from the Arabic world to medieval Europe where it became widespread. The Arabic tradition distinguishes 16 figures (al-ashkal) with their planetary, elemental, directional, seasonal, and binary properties; the treatise organizes these into systematic tables mapping each figure to its attributes. The tables in this Princeton MS — showing which figures are 'present' or 'absent', 'mobile' or 'stable', oriented 'east', 'west', 'north', or 'south' — are the operational core of the geomantic system, used to interpret horoscopic figure charts. The manuscript is a practical working reference rather than a philosophical treatise.

title: [Treatise on Charms and Talismans] (Princeton, Third Series no. 591, 1483 CE)
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public Domain — 1483 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 26-leaf Arabic manuscript treatise on charms and talismans (amulets), dated 1483 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 591). The MS contains multiple types of Islamic magical diagrams: pentagonal khatim talisman seals (pentagon star circles with Arabic numerals), red-bordered wafq letter grids, triangular staircase letter-combination tables (muhmal arrangements), and full-page diamond-lattice letter grids — all typical of the late medieval Arabic huruf/talisman tradition. The diamond-lattice grid (a diagonal crossing of letter-rows, producing a net of rhombus cells each containing an Arabic letter or combination) is a distinctive Islamic visual formula for encoding divine-name letter combinations in a spatially memorable way. The manuscript was compiled in 1483 CE, placing it in the same generation as the earliest European printed books and the high point of Ottoman imperial expansion — a period when Islamic talismanic manuscripts circulated widely across the Mediterranean and Middle East.

title: [Collection of Texts on Occult Sciences] (Princeton, Garrett no. 547H)
creator: Multiple authors (anthology)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript (date uncertain, 1700-1899 CE range). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A 230-page Arabic composite manuscript comprising seven texts on occult sciences (Garrett no. 547H), held at Princeton University Library. The collection includes a Zairja geomancy text (Risala fi 'Ilm al-Zairja — a sand-divination/letter divination hybrid system) identified in the incipit, alongside texts on astrology, letter science, numerology, and magical practices. The manuscript contains diagrammatic pages showing: numeric calculation tables for astrological/divinatory purposes, systematic jadwal (table) letter arrangements mapping Arabic letters to elemental and humoral properties, and elemental letter-speech tables assigning each Arabic letter to fire (nar), air (hawa), water (ma), or earth (turab) — the foundational classification of Arabic letters in the huruf/lettrism tradition. The Zairja ('taking out the concealed/inner meaning') is an Islamic divinatory system attributed to Idris (Hermes) that combines geomancy, letter science, and astrological calculation into a unified divinatory framework; it was described by Ibn Khaldun in the Muqaddima and represents the apex of Islamic learned divination. The Princeton composite codex preserves multiple independent occult texts in a single volume, typical of Ottoman-era compilation practice.

title: Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya — Oracle of the Abbasid Caliphs (Princeton, Garrett no. 551Hq)
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public Domain — Islamic manuscript, 1700-1835 CE. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: An oversize Arabic divination manuscript, 38 leaves (80 pages), held at Princeton University Library (Oversize Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 551Hq). The Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya Umara' al-Mu'minin (Oracle/Lottery of the Abbasid Caliphs, Commanders of the Faithful) is a systematic oracle book organized around the Abbasid Caliphs — each Caliph providing a set of verse-predictions in a two-column format for different query types. The MS is visually extraordinary: it contains seven full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle diagrams (dawa'ir) labeled by topic — Caliphs, Tribes, Women, Turks, Birds, Cities — and a grid page showing eight smaller oracle circles. These circles function as divinatory instruments: the querent follows a procedure involving letters and numbers (via the Zairja or qur'a system) to arrive at a specific cell in the concentric rings, which then directs them to the appropriate Caliph oracle section. Each circle has a gold or blue-grey decorative background in the outer ring, with alternating red and black Arabic text in the inner rings, and decorative cloud-curl corner ornaments. The combination of Islamic calligraphy, geometric diagrammatic precision, and cosmological structure makes these circles among the most visually striking Islamic divination diagrams in any collection.

title: Majmūʻ fī al-falak — Collection on Timekeeping and Astronomical Instruments (Princeton, Garrett no. 3442Y)
creator: Multiple authors (composite codex)
rights: Public Domain — 1533–1667 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A composite Arabic codex of 19 distinct texts on timekeeping and astronomical instruments (Majmū' fī al-Falak), 125 leaves, spanning 1533–1667 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 3442Y). The collection gathers short treatises on the sine quadrant (rub' al-mujib), the solar quadrant, the horoscope (ahkam al-nujum), the sundial, and related astronomical calculation methods. The manuscript contains texts by multiple authors in nastaliq and naskh hands, along with zodiac classification tables, calendar correlation tables, and numeric calculation grids. The zodiac tables — which appear near the end of the codex alongside astrological treatises — organize the 12 zodiac signs by their elemental qualities (fire, water, air, earth), humoral correspondences, and calendar placements, making the manuscript a working reference for Islamic timekeeping and astrological practice. One table correlates Persian month names (Farvardin through Isfand) with the zodiac signs they fall in and the number of days in each. These tables are typical of the jadwal tradition of Islamic scientific manuscripts — compact, grid-form visual summaries of information otherwise scattered across prose texts.

title: [Collection of Prayers and Talismans] (Princeton, Third Series no. 471, Sub-Saharan African)
creator: Anonymous (multiple authors/scribes)
rights: Public Domain — late manuscript material (1800-1999 CE). Princeton University Library.
blurb: A collection of 181 loose leaves (362 pages) of Sub-Saharan African Islamic manuscript material, 1800–1999 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 471). The leaves are housed between two pieces of animal skin and show significant damage from rodents and insects in the early folios. The manuscript contains prayers, invocations, descriptions and instructions for the use of talismans, amulets, and magic squares — the standard content of West African Islamic protective and divinatory manuscript practice known in the scholarship as the Qur'anic talisman tradition (kitab or hirz tradition). This tradition, widespread from Senegal through Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and across the Sahel, involves copying Qur'anic verses, divine name combinations, and wafq (magic square) grids onto paper (or leather, metal, cloth) as protective charms worn on the body or placed in the home. The Princeton collection preserves 181 separate leaves — not a bound codex but a cache of individual talisman pages — written in a bold, large-format West African Sudanic Arabic script characteristic of the Saharan and Sub-Saharan Islamic manuscript tradition. One leaf shows a remarkable full-page wafq magic square in a distinctive Sub-Saharan African style: a bordered grid with diagonal cross-hatching lines creating X-shaped subdivisions within each cell, and red (or orange-brown) Arabic text filling the triangular sub-cells. This visual formula — the cross-hatched wafq — is specific to West African talismanic manuscripts and is not found in Middle Eastern Islamic MS traditions.

title: Zād al-ashrāf fī wafq al-qāf — Treatise on the Letter Qāf and Its Wafq (Princeton, Garrett no. 335L)
creator: Khaṭṭāṭ, Ibrāhīm ibn Aḥmad (18th century)
rights: Public Domain — 19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A short Arabic manuscript treatise in five chapters on the magical properties of the letter qāf (ق) and its use in wafq (magic squares) and charms, 10 leaves (20 pages), 19th century, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 335L). The work is attributed to Ibrāhīm ibn Aḥmad al-Khaṭṭāṭ (the Calligrapher, 18th century). 'Ilm al-qāf — the science of the letter qaf — is a specialized branch of Arabic lettrism focusing on the 21st letter of the Arabic alphabet, whose abjad value is 100 and which occupies a particular position in the cosmological letter-science system: it is associated with the mountains that surround the world (Jabal Qaf, the cosmic mountain range in Islamic cosmology), with specific divine names, and with particular operative applications in talismanic practice. The treatise contains embedded wafq diagrams throughout: a 5×5 numeric magic square of the letter qaf, a 5×5 letter-arrangement wafq, a property/attribute table correlating the letter qaf's correspondences, and most spectacularly, a full-page labeled jadwal — the 'first of sixteen jadwal tables' (al-jadwal al-awwal min al-sita 'ashar jadwalan) — a large rectangular numeric grid occupying nearly the full page. The MS is written in naskh script with red ink used for chapter headings, emphasis, and the numerals/letters within the wafq cells.

title: Kunh al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʻdād — Treatise on Magic Squares (Princeton, Third Series no. 455)
creator: Ṭāʻūsī, Yaʻqūb ibn Muḥammad (also attr. Sharaf al-Dīn ʻAlī al-Yazdī, d. 1454)
rights: Public Domain — 18th–19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A Persian-language treatise on the construction and use of magic squares (wafq al-aʻdād), attributed to Yaʻqūb ibn Muḥammad al-Ṭāʻūsī and also to Sharaf al-Dīn ʻAlī al-Yazdī (d. 858/1454), organized in three sections (lawḥ). Held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 455), 89 leaves (178 pages), 18th–19th century CE, purchased from Smitskamp Oriental Antiquarian in 2001 and bound in red leather over paper boards with blind-stamped decoration. The manuscript is a systematic encyclopaedia of wafq construction, containing an extraordinary range of magic square formats: dense full-page letter-wafq grids where each cell is subdivided into sub-compartments and filled with Arabic letter combinations; large-cell numeric wafq in a sparse arithmetic-exposition format showing the raw integer values; combinatorial lookup tables for computing wafq parameters; labeled construction tables that reveal the derivation method step by step; multi-table pages presenting six or more wafq configurations simultaneously; and tricolor letter-wafq grids using red, black, and olive-green ink to color-code cells by magical correspondence category. Some tables are notched or L-shaped where the grid outgrew the page. The three-color wafq is characteristic of the Persianate tradition of color-coded wafq encyclopaedias; each full-page grid functions simultaneously as a mathematical object and a talismanic reference tool.

title: Sharḥ Manẓūmat Kashf al-Rān fī al-Zāyirjah — Commentary on the Zairja Divination System (Princeton, Garrett no. 542H)
creator: Anonymous (commentary; first text attr. tradition of Ibn al-ʻArabī)
rights: Public Domain — 1787 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: A volume of four texts on Islamic occult sciences, 39 leaves, dated 1787 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 542H). The manuscript was acquired from Brill in Leyden in 1900 from the library of Amīn ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ḥulwānī al-Madanī al-Ḥanafī (Medina) and donated to Princeton by Robert Garrett (Class of 1897) in 1942; it is bound in quarter leather with blue pastedowns and embossed vegetal motif paper. The first and main text (fol. 1a–15b) is a commentary on the Manẓūmat Kashf al-Rān fī al-Zāyirjah — a poem describing the Zairja, the Islamic divination instrument attributed to Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn al-ʻArabī (1165–1240 CE). The Zairja is a complex divinatory system that combines astrological letter correspondences, the abjad (letter-number) system, and wafq (magic square) computation to answer questions about the future: the practitioner converts the letters of a question into abjad values, identifies the relevant zodiac degree, and applies a table-based calculation procedure using a 4×4 or larger magic square to generate the answer. This manuscript preserves the computational apparatus of the Zairja in visual form: full-page numeric tables for the calculation procedure, multi-panel 4×4 magic square grids used as Saturn-square computation aids, angelic name abjad tables (giving the calculated values of Mīkā'īl, Hasmayīl, Ibfīshā'īl and related celestial intermediaries), column-addition verification arithmetic pages showing completed Zairja calculations, and two pages with distinctive muthallath (inverted triangle) text layout — a calligraphic format used for colophons and poetic conclusions.

title: Treatise on Ancient, Alchemical and Magical Alphabets (Princeton, Garrett no. 52B)
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public Domain — 18th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
blurb: An 18th-century Arabic manuscript treatise on 24 ancient, alchemical, and magical alphabet systems and their use in talismans and magical operations, 46 leaves, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 52B, Islamicmss). Acquired by Robert Garrett from Brill, Leyden, in 1925, from the books of Murād Bey Bārdūdī (Beirut); modern binding in violet paper over cardboard. The manuscript presents 24 distinct script systems — from the Language of Adam (the primordial tongue) to the Kufi script of the Caliph Umar period — each displayed as a full-page grid of letterforms: 28 cells (one per Arabic letter), red-ruled in a 7×4 arrangement, with each cell showing the equivalent symbol in the exotic script. Script systems represented include 'scripts of the soothsayers/diviners' (qalam al-kahanat/kahanira), Greco-Latin-adjacent systems (showing A, B, M, N, H, ∞, X analogs), occult letter-forms with Ψ, swastika, Π, and T motifs, the Qanawi script (associated with the Canaanites), the Fahlawi/Pahlavi script (Middle Persian), and branch-tally notation. Later sections introduce the 'Natural Script' (al-Qalam al-Tabi'i) — the theoretical root alphabet used to construct awfaq (magic squares) — shown as a numeric-decade correspondence table, and the 'Simat Scripts' (qalim al-simat) — talisman letter-forms tied to divine attributes. The treatise ends with a comparative chart showing six script systems in a single multi-column grid. This manuscript is a unique compendium of Islamic magical alphabet science, showing how diverse historical and legendary scripts were absorbed into the Islamic occult tradition as vehicles of talisman-making and letter-magic (ilm al-huruf).

title: Ghāyat al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʿdād — The Goal of Desire in the Composition of Magic Squares (Princeton, 1462 CE)
creator: Ṣūfī Kamāl Tustarī (active 14th century)
rights: Public Domain — 1462 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 1462 CE Persian manuscript copy of the Ghāyat al-Murād fī Wafq al-Aʿdād (The Ultimate Goal in Magic Square Composition), a comprehensive encyclopedic treatise on wafq (Islamic magic squares) by Ṣūfī Kamāl Tustarī (active 14th century). 131 digitized leaves (262 canvases), held at Princeton University Library (Islamicmss collection, figgy UUID edc0b2fe). This is one of the most systematic Islamic texts on wafq theory and practice: it covers the mathematical foundations of magic squares, the classification of wafq by planet, element, and magical operation, and the construction methods for numeric, letter-based, and combinatorial wafq grids. The manuscript is a later copy of a 14th-century original but is itself from 1462 CE, making it a 15th-century witness to a dense tradition of wafq scholarship. The treatise is notable for combining pure mathematical theory (properties of numbers, methods of construction) with magical application (which wafq to use for love, protection, healing, or harm), making it a bridge between Islamic mathematics and Islamic magic. The Princeton copy contains substantial annotations in the margins and a variety of diagram types: full-page dense letter wafq grids, large numeric magic squares in multiple configurations, and — unusually — an astrological operations table cross-referencing celestial figures with their spirit names, incenses, and magical effects, suggesting the manuscript contains more than one text or was bound with supplementary occult material.

title: ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt wa-Gharāʾib al-Mawjūdāt — Wonders of Creation (Princeton, Persian Illustrated MS)
creator: Zakarīyāʾ ibn Muḥammad al-Qazwīnī (1203–1283 CE, original text); anonymous illustrator
rights: Public Domain — 17th-18th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A finely illustrated Persian manuscript of Zakarīyāʾ al-Qazwīnī's ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt wa-Gharāʾib al-Mawjūdāt (Wonders of Creation and Marvels of Existing Things), 502 digitized pages, held at Princeton University Library. Al-Qazwīnī (1203–1283 CE) was a Persian-Arab cosmographer and geographer whose encyclopedic account of the wonders of the created world — organized from the celestial spheres down through terrestrial creatures, minerals, plants, and humans — became one of the most widely copied illustrated works in Islamic manuscript culture. This Princeton copy is a high-quality 17th or 18th century illustrated MS with full painted miniatures in Persian style accompanying the text sections. The jinn and supernatural beings section (late manuscript) contains a remarkable cluster of miniature paintings depicting Solomon (Sulaymān ʿalayhi al-salām) commanding the jinn — a central theme of Islamic cosmology in which the Prophet Solomon was granted dominion over humans, animals, wind, and the supernatural world of the jinn and demons. The paintings show Solomon flanked by human courtiers on one side and fantastic supernatural creatures (horned giants, black-bodied demons, animal-headed jinn, winged beings) on the other — visualizing the Quranic account of Solomon's army of jinn (Quran 21:82, 27:17, 34:12). The manuscript is associated with the figgy.princeton.edu digital library (UUID da45a495).

title: Kitāb Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Princeton, Garrett 3182Y, 19c Arabic)
creator: attributed to Ibn al-Ḥājj Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad (d. 1336); anonymous copyist (19th century)
rights: Public Domain — 19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 19th-century Arabic composite codex held at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 3182Y), covering the full range of Islamic occult sciences in thirty-plus chapters. Its title — Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Suns of Lights and Treasuries of Secrets) — signals its ambition: a comprehensive practitioner's treasury drawing on ʻilm al-ḥurūf (letter science), wafq (magic squares), practical talismanic operations, military magic, mineral alchemy, and geomantic divination for locating buried treasure. Unlike systematic theoretical treatises, this compendium presents knowledge as a step-by-step operational guide: each chapter names a divine attribute or magical goal and provides the associated wafq or sigil form, incense, ritual timing, and instructions. Diagrams appear in three distinct forms: (1) inline sigil illustrations using the 'shape like this' (صورة هكذا) convention, showing small drawn talisman forms directly in the running text; (2) embedded magic square grids (wafq) of 4×4 or larger format associated with specific divine names; (3) large operational jadwal (correspondence tables) correlating celestial or elemental categories with specific ritual actions; and (4) geometric divinatory diagrams for locating buried treasure (dafīna), showing a diamond-within-square sacred geometry template. Authorship is uncertain — the text has been attributed to Ibn al-Ḥājj (d. 1336) but may be later. Princeton University Library, Islamicmss collection, figgy UUID 567baddd.

title: Kitāb al-Ṭibb al-jadīd al-kimiyāʾī (Princeton, Islamic Mss, 17c Arabic/Ottoman)
creator: Ṣāliḥ Naṣr Allāh ibn Sallūm (d. ca. 1670s); after Paracelsus and Oswald Croll
rights: Public Domain — 17th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 17th-century composite codex at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts, figgy ff61422c), containing the Arabic translation of Paracelsian chemical medicine compiled by Ṣāliḥ Naṣr Allāh ibn Sallūm (d. ca. 1670s), who served as chief physician (hekimbaşı) to Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV. The text is one of the most important transmissions of Paracelsian iatrochemistry into the Islamic world, bringing the doctrines of Paracelsus (d. 1541) and Oswald Croll's Basilica chymica (1609) into Arabic and Ottoman Turkish. Ibn Sallūm's compilation interweaves Paracelsian theory (the tria prima of sulfur, mercury, salt; the doctrine of arcana; spagyric preparation of medicines) with Galenic and Islamic medical frameworks. The manuscript has three visually distinctive sections: (1) Arabic pharmaceutical treatise with dense Paracelsian theory and recipe descriptions; (2) a terminological section naming alchemical instruments and their uses (Fī asmāʾ al-ālāt, 'On the Names of Instruments') in a two-column format listing furnace types, retorts, and distillation apparatus; and (3) an Ottoman Turkish pharmaceutical formulary (late in the MS) with multiple compound medicine recipes in tabular format, showing ingredient names and dram/mithqal quantities in horizontal table entries — a practical addendum for pharmaceutical preparation. Princeton University Library, Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett collection, figgy UUID ff61422c.

title: Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn wa-al-jawhar al-maknūn (Princeton, Islamic Mss, 17c Arabic)
creator: attributed to al-Ghazzālī (1058–1111); described as extract from Kitāb al-Jafr of Imam ʻAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rights: Public Domain — 17th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 17th-century Arabic manuscript at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett collection, gift 1942; figgy 1626111a), titled Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn wa-al-jawhar al-maknūn (The Hidden Secret and the Concealed Gem). The text is attributed to al-Ghazzālī but describes itself in the preface as 'an extract from the Kitāb al-Jafr of the Imam ʻAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib' — placing it squarely in the Shia divinatory tradition of the Jafr (jabr), the legendary book of esoteric knowledge attributed to the fourth caliph Ali and later to Imam Jafar al-Sadiq (6th Imam, d. 765 CE). The manuscript consists of 54 leaves of paper with red frame-ruling and covers a numbered series of magical operations (The Third Operation, The Fourteenth Operation, etc.), each presenting a complete praxis: divine names and Quranic verses to recite, talisman forms to draw, ritual timing, materials (oud, saffron, frankincense), and the specific wafq (magic square) or geometric diagram to inscribe. The manuscript contains three categories of visual content: (1) embedded numeric magic squares (wafq) associated with the angel Gabriel and Quranic names, labeled at the corners with angelic designations; (2) geometric talisman diagrams drawn in red and black ink — most notably an X-cross-within-square form (the 'Fourteenth Operation') in which two diagonal lines in red divide a square into four angular sections, each section containing a letter value; (3) divination tables in Ottoman-influenced later additions near the end of the manuscript, containing numbered grid cells with geomantic marks. The text includes first-person testimonial passages in which Imam Jafar al-Sadiq describes using a specific wafq on a sultan and achieving his desired outcome — a narrative device common in the Jafr tradition to validate the efficacy of each operation. Princeton University Library, Garrett collection, figgy UUID 1626111a.

title: Seven Alchemy Texts — Lawh al-Dhahab and Six Further Treatises (Princeton Islamic MSS, 17c Arabic)
creator: anonymous compiler; authorities cited include Jabir ibn Hayyan (8–9c), al-Rāzī (854–925), Roger Bacon (1214–1292), Albertus Magnus (1200–1280)
rights: Public Domain — 17th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A 17th-century Arabic manuscript at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts collection, figgy 05fc8244) comprising seven complete alchemical treatises bound together in a single volume of 190 leaves (388 IIIF canvases). The first and primary treatise is Lawh al-Dhahab (لوح الذهب — The Gold Tablet), followed by six further treatises covering the full range of Jabirian practical alchemy: mercury operations (tadbīr al-zaybaq), sulphur treatments (tadbīr al-kibrīt), calcination of metals (taklīs al-dhahab / al-fiḍḍa / al-naḥs / al-zinj), sublimation, compound preparations, and theory of the balance (al-mīzān). The front matter of the codex is exceptional: it contains a multi-page detailed table of contents indexing operations by page number (fihrist), followed by two formal alchemical jadāwil (quality tables, fols. 4r–4v) — ruled grids that systematize each metal and mineral according to its degrees of the four Galenic qualities (hot/cold/wet/dry), in the tradition of Jabir ibn Hayyan's Mīzān (Balance) theory. The texts explicitly cite Jabir ibn Hayyan, al-Rāzī, Roger Bacon ('Rajār Bākūn'), and Albertus Magnus, reflecting the synthesis of Arabic and Latin alchemical traditions that characterized Ottoman-era scientific manuscripts. A distinctive feature of this MS is that the text throughout all seven treatises is written in a diagonal script orientation — alternating direction lines on each page — a compositional strategy unusual even among Arabic alchemical manuscripts. The opening page of the first treatise includes a 3×3 letter square with the letter pattern ن/و/ا (nūn/wāw/alif) forming a talisman-like grid, alongside ownership annotations. Princeton University Library, Islamic MSS, figgy UUID 05fc8244.

title: Astrological Compendium — Irshad-i Usturlāb and Seven Treatises (Princeton OPenn Islamic MSS, Persian 1670)
creator: primary: Nāṣir ibn Ḥaydar (Irshād-i Usṭurlāb); further: Abū Al-Khayr Muḥammad Taqī Fārsī (Maṭāliʻʹnāmah); tradition of Abū Maʻshar
rights: Public Domain — 1670 CE Persian manuscript. Princeton University Library.
blurb: A Persian astrological compendium copied in 1670 CE (AH 1081), comprising seven treatises on astrology, the astrolabe, astronomical tables, and astrological judgment (Princeton University Library, OPenn Islamic Manuscripts, figgy 68f32e92, ark:/88435/dc41687w42j). The primary work is Irshād-i Usṭurlāb (Guidance on the Astrolabe) by Nāṣir ibn Ḥaydar; further treatises cover lunar eclipses, planetary risings and settings, astronomical tables (zīj), Maṭāliʻʹnāmah (Book of Ascendants) by Abū Al-Khayr Muḥammad Taqī Fārsī, and astrological judgments drawn from the tradition of Abū Maʻshar. The manuscript is written in elegant Persian nastaʻlīq script with extensive red-ink rubrication marking chapter headings and key technical terms. The codex is physically extraordinary: bound in fine black leather with elaborate gold-tooled mandorla binding — a large polylobed central medallion (shamseh) surrounded by arabesque filigree tooling on both front and back covers, with cartouches containing calligraphic owner inscriptions on the vertical axis. Two smaller diamond cartouches and a chain-pattern gilt border complete the design. The binding bears the name Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad Bāqir on the pendant cartouches. The manuscript passed through distinguished later ownership: it belonged to Muḥammad ʻAlī al-Iṣfahānī, then to Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan (the Swiss-based diplomat and art collector who assembled one of the finest Islamic manuscript libraries of the 20th century), and was acquired by Lawrence J. Schoenberg in 2001 before reaching Princeton. The front matter includes an ownership leaf (fol. 1r) covered with astrological calculations and multiple owner seals from its provenance chain, and the text contains a formal astrological planetary classification table (fol. 78r) with symbolic planetary headers and six rows of descriptive text for each planet's characteristics.

title: Compendium Maleficarum — Guazzo's Demonological Woodcut Cycle (1608/1626)
creator: Francesco Maria Guazzo; woodcuts anonymous (Milan, 1608)
rights: Public Domain — 1608 CE printed book illustrations. Francesco Maria Guazzo. Photographs from Internet Archive.
blurb: The visual compendium of early modern witchcraft iconography. Francesco Maria Guazzo's *Compendium Maleficarum* (first edition Milan 1608; second edition Milan 1626) is a Dominican friar's systematic demonological treatise illustrated by a cycle of 22 engraved woodcuts that constituted the most comprehensive and widely reproduced visual catalogue of witchcraft practices in the early modern period. Unlike the earlier *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486), which had no illustrations, Guazzo's work presented each category of diabolical act — the pact with the Devil, the mark, apostasy, the sabbath with dancing and feasting, weather magic, killing cattle, flight by broomstick and on animals, transformation, harmful magic and maleficium — as a distinct engraved scene. The woodcuts drew on the accumulated tradition of witch imagery established by Hans Baldung Grien (1510), Dürer (1498–1500), and the artist of the *Champion des Dames* (c. 1451), but systematized that tradition into a numbered demonological typology directly keyed to the text's chapter structure. The 1626 edition reproduced the same woodcut cycle as 1608 with minor variations. Guazzo's work was compiled during the height of the witch trials and was used as an authority in Italian, Spanish, and German courts. The woodcuts became the canonical visual reference for sabbath, pact, and maleficium iconography in subsequent demonological literature and persist as the primary visual source for academic study of early modern witchcraft belief.

blurb: Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Secret Figures of the Rosicrucians, Altona 1785-88) is the central emblematic compendium of the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order — an 18th-century Rosicrucian brotherhood. Compiled by the order and attributed to Hinricus Madathanus Theosophus (Adrian von Mynsicht), it presents a systematic visual curriculum integrating Paracelsian alchemy, Kabbalistic mysticism, and Christian theology through elaborate symbolic diagrams encoding initiate doctrine on the three realms (Physica, Metaphysica, Hyperphysica). The most elaborately illustrated Rosicrucian text of the 18th century.

title: Aurora Consurgens — Zentralbibliothek Zürich Ms. Rh. 172
creator: Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas (attr.); illuminator unknown (Rhineland or Basel workshop, c. 1420)
rights: Public Domain. Manuscript c. 1420, well outside copyright. Digital images from e-codices Virtual Manuscript Library of Switzerland (e-codices.ch), CC BY-NC 4.0.
blurb: One of the most important early alchemical manuscripts in the West, the Aurora Consurgens (c. 1420, ZBZ Ms. Rh. 172) contains 38 color miniatures among the earliest known systematic alchemical illustrations. The text, attributed to Thomas Aquinas though now considered pseudo-Thomist, allegorizes the alchemical process through the imagery of the Song of Songs and Proverbs, identifying the Philosopher's Stone with the divine Sapientia (Wisdom). Its miniatures — depicting the dragon in the vessel, the Sol-Luna coniunctio, the blackened Sapientia with solar radiance, and the lion-eagle combat — are foundational documents in the visual history of Western esotericism, analyzed definitively by Barbara Obrist and Marie-Louise von Franz.
